text:
📺 “Navy Medic Abducted by 15-Foot-Tall Praying Mantis Aliens: The Kevin Kammann Story”
🗓️ Published September 19, 2026
🔗 https://t.co/TkgCVkbDhQ
🕵🏻‍♂️ Preston Dennett — UFO Researcher
👤 Kevin Kammann
🗓️ Abduction: 1982, probably during the summer
⛴️ USS San Bernardino (LST-1189)

Kevin Kammann — The Account of an Encounter with “Praying Mantis” Beings

In the documentary “Navy Medic Abducted by 15-Foot-Tall Praying Mantis Aliens: The Kevin Kammann Story,”Preston Dennett reconstructs the extraordinary experience reported by former U.S. Navy corpsman Kevin Lee Kammann. Dennett emphasizes that Kevin said he experienced the encounter consciously and that his memories were not recovered through hypnosis.

Kevin Kammann and Jeff Reich

Kevin Kammann was born in 1954 and grew up in Kankakee, Illinois, with his fraternal twin brother, Kim. After graduating from high school in 1972, he worked at a hospital and developed an interest in medicine. He joined the U.S. Navy on February 28, 1973, and received medical training at Camp Pendleton.

After a break in his service, Kevin returned to the Navy in 1978 and was assigned as a hospital corpsman aboard the USS San Bernardino (LST-1189).

The first person he met aboard the ship was Jeff Reich, a personnel clerk from Gary, Indiana. The two shared a compartment and soon became close friends, even spending some of their leave time together.

After about four years of Navy service together, Jeff made an astonishing revelation. He claimed that he had been in contact with extraterrestrial beings since he was about ten years old. According to Jeff, he had been taken aboard their craft many times, had visited their planet and other places, and could communicate with them mentally.

Kevin was initially extremely skeptical. As a corpsman, he even wondered whether Jeff should undergo a psychiatric evaluation.

Jeff Describes Kevin’s Home — But in the Past

A few days later, Jeff told Kevin that his “friends” had taken him to Kevin’s family home in Kankakee, even though both men were thousands of miles away.

Jeff began describing very specific details of the house. According to Kevin, he knew things he should have had no way of knowing, including a 1966 Ford Galaxie 500, a chocolate milkshake stain on its back seat, the furniture, carpeting, kitchen, Kevin’s bedroom, and even things that had been written on the bedroom walls.

But there was an even stranger aspect to Jeff’s description: he was not describing the house as it existed at that time. He was describing it as it had appeared ten to fifteen years earlier.

The Ford, for example, had been sold in 1970, and much of the furniture and carpeting Jeff described had been gone for more than a decade.

Kevin began wondering whether there might actually be something behind his friend’s claims.

He finally challenged Jeff:

“Okay, then I want to meet your little green friends.”

Jeff said he would ask them.

The Arrival of the Craft

A few days later, Jeff told Kevin that the beings had agreed to give him a ride.

Kevin still assumed his friend was joking. Then, one day shortly before noon, Jeff told him that they had arrived and instructed him to go up on deck.

Kevin went outside and said he saw a gigantic craft hovering near the USS San Bernardino.

He described it as enormously larger than the ship, completely silent and glowing with brilliant colors — red, yellow, green, purple, orange and others. He compared its appearance to an enormous illuminated diamond.

Even stranger was the apparent reaction of the other sailors: nobody seemed to notice it.

Kevin attempted to attract the attention of a ship’s cook named Brooks, who was talking with another sailor named Davis. Kevin said he even grabbed or shook Brooks’s arm and pointed toward the enormous object, but Brooks did not respond.

Then Kevin experienced what he described as a sudden “shift.”

He was no longer standing on the deck.

Aboard the Craft

Kevin said he suddenly found himself physically inside the craft.

The walls appeared solid but seemed to become transparent wherever he looked through them. He could see the ocean below and the USS San Bernardino becoming smaller and smaller.

His immediate thought was that he was now AWOL.

A male voice answered him telepathically:

“No, you’re not. They don’t even know you’re gone.”

Another voice reportedly told him:

“Yes, it is. It’s what you wanted.”

Kevin then looked toward the ship and described something especially difficult for him to understand: he could apparently see himself still standing on the deck, attempting to get Brooks’s attention.

It seemed as though he was somehow in two places at once.

Returning to Kankakee

Kevin felt no acceleration or conventional movement. Instead, the scenery simply changed.

He suddenly recognized Kankakee.

The craft stopped near the bank building where his father worked. Kevin said he could see through the walls of the building, observing its internal structures until he located his father.

They then moved over the church/school where his mother taught. Again, Kevin said he could see through the building and watch his mother teaching.

The beings reportedly told him telepathically that his parents were honorable people and had done a good job raising him.

Once again, however, Kevin had the impression that he was not simply observing the present. The beings appeared capable of showing him events from the past.

Above the Moon

Another sudden shift occurred.

Kevin saw a dark, gray, cratered landscape beneath the craft. At first, he thought he was looking at some kind of military bombing range on Earth.

Then the craft moved over a ridge.

Kevin saw Earth hanging in space.

He described it as appearing about the size of a tennis ball and realized that he was above the Moon.

The experience seemed so impossible that Kevin pinched the back of his hand hard enough to make himself bleed, hoping to leave a physical mark that might prove to him later that the experience had not simply been a dream.

At another point, he said he was taken into the past again and shown his own home. He saw himself as a boy of about twelve, talking with his grandmother, who would later die in 1972.

The Telepathic Conversation

Kevin began asking the beings questions.

He still had not turned around to look directly at them. He heard their responses telepathically, in perfectly understandable English, but described the voices as monotone and almost emotionless.

When Kevin asked where they came from, a kind of three-dimensional star map appeared around him.

He recognized the Solar System and some of its planets. A distant location was then indicated as the beings’ place of origin.

According to Kevin, they told him that they came from approximately six light-years away and that their journey to Earth took about three and a half months.

Kevin said he could neither remember nor reproduce the name of their planet or species because the sounds were completely unfamiliar to him.

The beings also claimed to understand all human languages and dialects, including languages that had been extinct for thousands of years.

Why They Were Observing Humanity

Kevin asked why they were on Earth.

According to his account, the beings said they had been here for a very long time and were primarily here to observe.

They said they did not interfere with humanity’s religions or politics.

At the same time, however, Kevin said they told him that they interacted with the U.S. government and other major governments around the world. They also reportedly mentioned four other species that interacted with human governments.

Kevin further recalled being told that the Roswell crash was real and that these beings were capable of cloaking themselves.

These statements are part of what Kevin said he was told during the encounter.

Nuclear Weapons and the “Countdown Clock”

One of the most important subjects of the conversation concerned atomic weapons.

According to Kevin, the beings explained that when humanity developed and began testing nuclear weapons in 1945, they and other extraterrestrial species began paying much closer attention to humans.

They reportedly told him that the explosion of the atomic bomb had started a:

“countdown clock.”

They did not clearly explain what the phrase meant. Kevin nevertheless came away with the impression that it referred to some potentially catastrophic scenario.

Images of Past, Present and Future Disasters

The beings then showed Kevin a series of extraordinarily vivid three-dimensional scenes.

He described seeing mudslides, volcanic eruptions, hurricanes, floods, wars, explosions, destruction and large numbers of people being killed.

Kevin said some of what he was shown belonged to the past, some to the present, and some apparently to the future.

Throughout the display, the beings reportedly repeated:

“Some of what you see has already been. Some of what you see has yet to be. These are things that are going to come. The destiny will be fulfilled.”

Kevin said the scenes did not appear like ordinary images on a screen. They looked completely real, almost as though he were actually present and watching the events unfold.

The Vision of His Motorcycle Accident

Among the images shown to Kevin was one that concerned him personally.

He saw an older version of himself riding a motorcycle. An automobile struck him broadside, throwing him to the ground. Kevin saw himself lying there completely motionless.

At the time, he interpreted the vision as showing him how he would die.

For years afterward, the image remained in the back of his mind.

Then, in 2003, Kevin purchased a 100th Anniversary Harley-Davidson Sportster. He later recalled that he had felt uneasy about buying the motorcycle precisely because of what he had been shown in 1982. But he had always wanted a 100th Anniversary Harley, and when his sister-in-law offered to buy it for him under a payment arrangement that was too good to pass up, he accepted.

Kevin owned the Harley for exactly 14 days.

On the fifteenth day, while returning from his brother’s home, a driver made an illegal U-turn and struck Kevin broadside.

Kevin was thrown from the motorcycle and knocked unconscious.

When he regained consciousness, his lower left leg had been shattered.

He underwent surgery the following day and later described having a metal plate and 11 screws placed in his leg. The recovery was extremely long: Kevin said it took 22 months for the bones to heal, followed by approximately another year on crutches.

When Kevin later discussed the accident with Preston, he explained that he then realized what he believed he had been shown back in 1982.

The beings had not shown him his death. In Kevin’s interpretation, they had shown him the motorcycle accident that would actually happen to him 21 years later.

The parallels deeply affected him: the motorcycle, being struck broadside by a car, losing consciousness, and seeing himself motionless on the ground.

Despite the severity of the accident and the lengthy recovery, Kevin eventually improved enough to consider riding the motorcycle again.

“We’re Not Little and We’re Not Green”

Until this point in the experience, Kevin had still not found the courage to turn around and look directly at the beings communicating with him.

Eventually, he asked what they looked like.

They replied:

“We’re not little and we’re not green.”

They also warned him that their appearance might frighten him.

Kevin finally decided to look.

The Three “Praying Mantis” Beings

Kevin described entering or looking into an extremely bright white area containing panels and devices that seemed strangely primitive compared with the extraordinary technology he had already witnessed.

There were three enormous white throne-like chairs.

The chairs turned toward him.

Sitting in them were three gigantic humanoid beings resembling praying mantises.

One stood up.

Kevin estimated its height at approximately 15 feet, or more than four meters.

He described the beings as having:

milky-white skin;
extremely thin bodies;
extraordinarily long, slender arms and legs;
three claw-like fingers;
enormous heads;
gigantic black eyes, roughly triangular in appearance;
no obvious external ears or conventional nose;
facial structures that reminded him strongly of a praying mantis.

Kevin said their heads were enormously larger than human heads and that their eyes appeared larger than basketballs.

He also described an especially unusual feature: parts of their heads appeared partially transparent, allowing him, he believed, to see internal structures, including their brains and blood flowing inside them.

Despite being terrified by their appearance, Kevin believed he was looking at highly intelligent beings.

The Invitation to Visit Their Planet

One of the beings approached Kevin.

It asked whether he would like to visit their planet.

By this point, Kevin’s curiosity had turned into fear. He felt trapped and declined the invitation.

When the being placed a claw-like hand on his shoulder, Kevin panicked and attempted to fight back.

He then lost consciousness.

Back Aboard the USS San Bernardino

The next thing Kevin remembered was finding himself back inside his compartment aboard the USS San Bernardino, covered in sweat.

Jeff was standing there.

Smiling, he said:

“So, tell me about your ride.”

Kevin became furious.

The experience had terrified him, and his relationship with Jeff effectively ended. Kevin even began wondering whether his former friend might somehow be one of the beings in disguise.

After their time aboard the ship, Kevin would never see Jeff again.

The Mystery of Brooks and Davis

Kevin later attempted to determine what had happened while he believed he had been aboard the craft.

He approached Brooks, the cook whose attention he had tried to attract when the enormous object appeared.

Kevin reminded Brooks of the conversation he had been having with Davis on deck and asked whether he remembered Kevin trying to speak to him.

Brooks’s response shocked him.

Brooks remembered his conversation with Davis but insisted that Kevin had not been there. He denied that Kevin had grabbed or shaken his arm.

Kevin then questioned Davis and received essentially the same response.

This was particularly strange to Kevin because, while aboard the craft, he believed he had looked down and seen himself standing on the deck near Brooks and Davis.

The Disappearance of the Memories

After the encounter, something unusual began happening to Kevin’s memory.

Much of the experience gradually faded.

He knew that something extraordinary had happened. He remembered being taken aboard a UFO and retained the feeling that the encounter had been deeply frightening, but many of the details became inaccessible.

Kevin remained aboard the USS San Bernardino for another two years before leaving military service.

Jeff disappeared from his life.

A Praying Mantis on Television

Several years later, in the late 1980s, Kevin was watching television when a close-up image of a praying mantisappeared on the screen.

According to Kevin, the image triggered an immediate reaction.

The “wall” blocking his memories suddenly collapsed, and within minutes much of the experience came flooding back.

He remembered the invitation, the craft, the journey, the conversations and, most importantly, the beings themselves.

Kevin then faced the opposite problem: he could not stop thinking about the experience.

He decided to tell his family. According to Kevin, his family was understanding and believed him, although he also received ridicule from friends and acquaintances.

Events Kevin Believed He Recognized Later

As the years passed, Kevin continued thinking about the disasters he said had been shown to him.

When major hurricanes and other catastrophes occurred, he sometimes wondered whether they were among the events he had seen aboard the craft.

In 2005, while watching television coverage of a deadly mining disaster, Kevin said he experienced another powerful sense of recognition. He turned to his wife and told her:

“I’ve seen this before. They showed me this on the UFO.”

For Kevin, events such as these, together with his motorcycle accident, reinforced his conviction that the 1982 experience had been real.

He also said that the top of his left hand still carried a faint scar from where he had pinched himself while above the Moon. Later, he noticed marks on his leg that he considered unusual and wondered whether there might have been additional aspects of the encounter that he still could not consciously remember.

Kevin Decides to Tell His Story

Over the years, Kevin became increasingly determined to make his experience public.

He believed that people had a right to hear what he had experienced, regardless of whether they chose to believe him.

Preston Dennett eventually documented Kevin’s case in his book Inside UFOs: True Accounts of Contact and helped bring Kevin’s testimony to a wider audience through interviews and radio appearances. Kevin also appeared on Japanese television and spoke publicly about the encounter.

Dennett personally interviewed Kevin in July 2007.

The documentary includes this extensive interview, allowing Kevin to describe much of the experience in his own words, rather than having the entire story related only through Preston’s narration.

Kevin also emphasized that, as far as he knew, this was his only UFO encounter of this kind and that he had no desire to experience anything like it again.

His twin brother Kim, however, reportedly had anomalous experiences of his own, involving beings described differently, as “Greys.”

Kevin ultimately described the encounter as a life-altering experience. Regardless of how other people reacted to his story, he remained convinced that what had happened to him was real.

One of the lessons he drew from it was expressed in a simple warning:

“Be careful what you ask for because you just might get it.”

Kevin Kammann’s Death

Kevin continued for years to speak about the experience and to express his desire for the story to be known.

Kevin Lee Kammann died on April 8, 2021, at the age of 66.

His testimony survives through the interviews he recorded, Preston Dennett’s work, and the accounts in which Kevin described what he believed happened to him aboard the USS San Bernardino in 1982.

The Major Unresolved Element: Jeff Reich

One of the most important unresolved elements of the entire story remains Jeff Reich.

Jeff is not a secondary character.

He is the person who claimed to have been in contact with these beings since childhood. He is the one who said he had repeatedly traveled aboard their craft and had even visited their planet. He is the one who described Kevin’s childhood home with remarkable accuracy, but as it had existed many years earlier.

Jeff communicated Kevin’s request to meet the beings. Jeff announced that they had arrived. And when Kevin suddenly found himself back in his compartment, Jeff appeared to already know exactly what had happened, asking him:

“So, tell me about your ride.”

An independent account from Jeff would therefore be extremely valuable. It could allow his memories to be compared with Kevin’s testimony and reveal which elements of their accounts matched, which differed, and what Jeff might remember independently about the events.

Preston Dennett has not yet been able to locate Jeff, but he will continue searching for him.

Kevin can no longer participate in such a comparison, but his testimony has been preserved through his recorded interviews and Preston Dennett’s documentation of the case.

Meteor Crater in Arizona, formed roughly 50,000 years ago by an iron-nickel meteorite about 160 feet (50 metres) across, and includes shaky handheld video from the rim showing the crater's vast scale and depth.

The impact occurred during the Pleistocene epoch in a cooler, wetter landscape inhabited by mammoths and giant ground sloths, excavating a bowl nearly 1.2 kilometres wide and initially over 200 metres deep.

As one of Earth's best-preserved impact sites, it offers valuable data on crater formation processes and asteroid hazards, with most of the original meteorite vaporised on impact.

6. Recommendations
Draft model legislation that mirrors Chapter 253D structure, substituting violence terminology and defining “course of harmful violent conduct” as two or more incidents.
Convene a working group of law-enforcement executives, prosecutors, clinicians, and corrections officials to refine operational criteria and risk-assessment protocols.
Authorize a limited pilot in selected jurisdictions with independent evaluation of public-safety outcomes and costs.
Align any new program with existing Mentally Ill and Dangerous provisions (Chapter 253B) to avoid fragmentation.
Conclusion
The Violently Dangerous Persons Act offers a direct, constitutionally grounded extension of Minnesota’s existing civil-commitment framework. By focusing on a documented course of violent behavior rather than solely on criminal convictions, and by applying the same clear-and-convincing standard and indeterminate-treatment model already used for sexually dangerous persons, the Act provides law enforcement and the courts with an additional tool for managing individuals whose risk profile exceeds ordinary correctional supervision. International precedent and domestic experience with sex-offender civil commitment suggest the approach is both feasible and potentially transformative. Independent modeling indicating a 60–64 percent reduction in violence warrants serious examination by policymakers, practitioners, and researchers.
References (selected)
Minnesota Statutes Chapter 253D (Civil Commitment and Treatment of Sex Offenders).
Minnesota Statutes § 253D.02, subd. 16 (definition of sexually dangerous person).
Relevant comparative literature on preventive detention (Germany § 66 StGB), Australian continuing detention orders, and New Zealand Public Safety (Public Protection Orders) Act 2014.
U.S. state sexually violent predator statutes (approximately 20 states + District of Columbia).

text:
You can walk into a Catholic church almost anywhere on earth and know exactly where you are.

You could be in Rome, Poland, Kenya, Mexico, the Philippines, or sitting in a nearly empty parish in Chester County on a Tuesday morning. You may not understand a word being spoken, but you will still recognize the Mass. You will know when to stand, when to kneel, what is happening at the altar, and why everyone came.

That alone is incredible. But then you remember what it took for the Mass to survive.

It was offered in catacombs when Christians had to hide. It was offered in prison camps, during wars, in Irish homes when the faith was persecuted, and in underground churches where being caught could cost people everything. Priests risked their lives to celebrate it. Catholics risked theirs just to be there.

Kings died. Empires collapsed. Borders changed. Whole countries disappeared.

The Mass continued.

And now I get to walk into my church on an ordinary weekday morning and step into the same worship Catholics have carried across centuries.

That is what gets me.

Catholicism is not tied to one country, one culture, one preacher, or one generation. The Church is bigger than all of that.

You can cross an ocean, walk through the doors of a Catholic church, and still know exactly where you are.

WWE Unreal is a professional wrestling documentary and reality series on Netflix that provides an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the creative process and internal operations of WWE.

WWE Unreal

Show Overview

Genre: Reality television / Documentary series.

Premise: The series follows WWE Superstars and executives, notably Paul "Triple H" Levesque, as they plan storylines in the writers' room and manage the "Gorilla Position" during live broadcasts.

Production: A collaboration between WWE, Omaha Productions (Peyton Manning), NFL Films, and Skydance Sports.

Seasons & Episodes

The series has released two seasons as of January 2026:

Season 1: Premiered July 29, 2025. It chronicled the lead-up to the debut of WWE Raw on Netflix and WrestleMania 41. Notable segments included a look at John Cena's high-profile storyline turns and the return of Charlotte Flair.

Season 2: Released January 20, 2026. This five-episode season focuses on the "Road to SummerSlam 2025" and features superstars like Seth Rollins, Becky Lynch, Rhea Ripley, and Cody Rhodes.

It delves into real-life drama such as R-Truth's contract negotiations and Naomi's previous walkout from the company.

Season 3: Confirmed to be in development, expected to focus on John Cena's retirement tour.

Key Personalities Featured

Executives: Paul "Triple H" Levesque (Narrator), Peyton Manning (Executive Producer).

Superstars: John Cena, Roman Reigns, Cody Rhodes, CM Punk, Rhea Ripley, Becky Lynch, Seth Rollins, and Bianca Belair.

text:
Another Yemen Podcast from my favorite podcaster @osamaalqutaibi, with two prominent journalists, @YemenShababNet’s @dubalh and @BelqeesTV’s @AhmadALzurqa, to discuss how the Houthis won on the West Coast.

Ahmed: “We defeated ourselves before Iran defeated us.”

Abdullah: “Iran turned the Houthi militia into a state, while our allies turned us from a state into something resembling a militia.”

Part I.

The podcast asks three connected questions. Why did Mocha and Bab al-Mandab fall? What are the Houthis doing with their gains? And what would have to change for their opponents to recover?

Abdullah and Ahmed do not offer a single explanation for the collapse. They describe a combination of battlefield pressure, divided command, political competition, dependence on outside support, and decisions that were not made when the front was still holding. They also discuss allegations of betrayal and deliberate Saudi inaction. Those allegations are part of the conversation, but neither journalist establishes them as solid facts.

Abdullah draws the distinction at the outset. “We said it was not a handover or betrayal. But it was not normal either. It was incapacity and failure.”

His account begins before the final Houthi breakthrough. He says the West Coast had been under sustained attack for weeks, with missiles and drones inflicting losses that were not fully disclosed. The Houthis initially pressed the northern positions around Hays and Al-Khokha before breaking through at Al-Barh. The loss of Al-Barh junction was followed by the fall of Khalid bin al-Walid camp. Once Houthi forces reached a command-and-control center behind the forward positions, the danger of encirclement spread across the defensive line.

The withdrawals that followed made the collapse look sudden, but Abdullah argues that its causes were much older. “There was incapacity and failure more than betrayal.”

The West Coast @NRFYemen forces had been assembled under @modgovae sponsorship from three main components: southern fighters @SouthArmed @alamalikah, Tihami resistance forces, and Tariq Saleh @tarikyemen's National Resistance. The UAE provided a common authority and much of the organization that allowed these formations to operate together. When it withdrew, the forces remained, but their separate loyalties, command arrangements, and political interests did not disappear.

Abdullah credits the Emiratis with earlier military gains. His criticism is that they moved from building a fighting force to building political influence before the military project was complete. He points to the Southern Transitional Council @STCSouthArabia and the National Resistance Political Bureau @P_B_N_R as examples of political ambitions overtaking military priorities. “Rushing the transition from military work to political work ruined both,” he says.

Ahmed is equally critical of what happened after the UAE’s departure. He argues that the Houthi attack was foreseeable, yet the government, Tariq Saleh, and Saudi Arabia @modgovksa failed to prepare a coordinated defense. The Taiz and West Coast fronts were connected geographically but divided operationally. Forces holding positions around Jabal Habashi and other areas answered to different commands from those farther west.

The claim that the armed forces @YemenMOD had been unified does not convince him. “Perhaps on paper. Administratively, they were integrated. Operationally, there was a very serious failure.”

That is one of the clearest explanations in the discussion. The problem was not simply whether there were enough brigades or enough fighters. It was whether anyone could direct them as a single force when the Houthis attacked. 

Ahmed raises allegations about personnel records, undisclosed military facilities, and the deterioration of trust between Saudi officers and Tariq Saleh. 

Abdullah describes the Houthis concentrating fighters and firepower against weak points along an extended defensive line. He says Houthi drones targeted artillery crews and supporting Multiple Launch Rocket System (MLRS) units, weakening the infantry’s ability to hold its positions. Abdullah also argues that Saudi air cover was largely absent during crucial periods. Ahmed agrees that air support mattered but insists that its absence cannot explain away the failures of preparation and command.

The discussion then turns to the allegation that Saudi Arabia deliberately allowed the West Coast to fall. The journalists consider whether Riyadh distrusted Tariq because of his Emirati ties and whether Saudi decision-makers wanted to reduce his military independence. Ahmed raises a further theory: that a Houthi advance to Bab al-Mandab might force the international community to confront the group and shift some of the burden away from Saudi Arabia.

Abdullah places more emphasis on indecision and failure. “If Saudi Arabia had been serious about preventing Mocha’s fall, it could have done so with its own capabilities, without American intervention,” he argues. That is his assessment of what Saudi Arabia could have done, not proof that intervention would necessarily have changed the outcome.

The journalists are particularly angry about what happened to the men left behind. They describe fighters stranded during the withdrawal, personnel on the islands without adequate evacuation arrangements, and soldiers who were captured or abandoned. They accuse the government and military leadership of failing to take responsibility for those who had fought under their command.

Ahmed asks where the operations room was and who was responsible for the men left exposed. He argues that leaders were preoccupied with explaining the defeat instead of accounting for their forces and rebuilding them. In his telling, the loss cannot be assigned to Tariq alone. Responsibility extends to the government and the coalition because all had a role in the military structure that collapsed.

The podcast also discusses large numbers of dead, captured, and displaced people. These figures are estimates given during the conversation rather than independently established totals. Abdullah describes the effect on Tihami communities whose members had fought for years and on families forced to flee yet again. The human consequences make the debate about command and responsibility more than an argument between political factions.

The first part of the conversation ultimately challenges the idea that the fall of Mocha can be explained by one dramatic moment. The Houthi breakthrough mattered, but the journalists argue that the military system had been weakened by years of divided authority and unfinished institution-building. The retreat revealed those weaknesses all at once.

Part II. 

The second part of the conversation turns from the collapse to the territory the Houthis have gained. Abdullah describes a coastal strip running through Hays, Al-Khokha, Mocha, and Dhubab toward Bab al-Mandab. He says the Houthis reached the strait and moved onto islands, including Perim, also known as Mayyun. His description is a claim about the battlefield at the time of the recording, not an independently verified map of control.

Abdullah is careful about the Kahbub mountains, which overlook the strait from the landward side. He says the Houthis are fighting the Southern Giants Brigades there and have not secured the entire area. “It is still a contested area, with advances and retreats between them and the government forces,” he explains. Abdullah considers the heights more consequential than simply occupying exposed coastal ground because of the military leverage they could provide over the passage. 

He also cautions against confusing a dramatic territorial announcement with the completion of a military operation. Abdullah describes the initial Houthi presence in parts of the newly captured territory as relatively light and suggests that publicity surrounding the advance may have run ahead of consolidation. His concern is what happens if the Houthis are given time to entrench themselves.

The discussion then widens to Taiz and Ma'rib. Abdullah believes the Houthis will first try to secure their gains around Mocha and Bab al-Mandab. He then describes possible pressure eastward from Kahbub toward Al-Turbah and the routes serving Taiz, alongside pressure toward the Safer oil facilities in Ma'rib. These are the objectives he anticipates, not confirmed plans. His argument is that the West Coast cannot be understood in isolation from the other fronts.

Ahmed makes the same point through the contrast in command structures. He says the Houthis have “one operations room, one decision, one movement,” allowing them to apply pressure from Taiz to Al-Bayda while their opponents remain divided. He also argues that the Houthis benefit from Iranian military support and from their opponents' inability to build an equally coherent force. His criticism is directed as much at the government and its allies as at the Houthis themselves.

One of the sharpest exchanges comes when the journalists compare the two sides' military development. Abdullah says, “Iran turned the Houthi militia into a state, while our allies turned us from a state into something resembling a militia.” It is a deliberately stark criticism of the way outside powers have supported competing Yemeni formations. He argues that the Houthis have developed missiles and drones while government-aligned forces have remained constrained by decisions made in Riyadh and Abu Dhabi.

The conversation also examines the Houthis' attempt to reassure foreign governments after reaching Bab al-Mandab. The speakers discuss statements suggesting that navigation would remain open and that the Houthis' immediate dispute was with Saudi Arabia. Abdullah compares this approach to the group's earlier assurances to tribes in Amran, arguing that limited promises can help a force consolidate control before its position changes. He sums up his skepticism in one sentence. “Whoever can permit passage can also prevent it.”

The podcast does not establish that the Houthis have made a secret deal with Washington or any other government. The journalists discuss reported communications and speculate about what the Houthis may be offering in exchange for international restraint. They also consider whether pressure at Bab al-Mandab is connected to Iran's confrontation with the United States around the Strait of Hormuz. Those are interpretations of regional strategy, not demonstrated agreements.

For Abdullah, the broader cost is that each territorial gain makes the next confrontation harder. “Every time the Houthis take a commanding or strategic area, their appetite grows, and they begin working on the next area,” he argues. He says recapturing lost territory is possible but becomes more costly the longer the Houthis are allowed to consolidate it.

Ahmed also worries about the psychological effect of the defeat. The idea that the Houthis cannot be beaten becomes stronger with each collapse, while accusations of betrayal spread among the forces opposing them. The journalists connect this loss of confidence to a much wider failure of government. They describe unpaid salaries, poor treatment of displaced families, and armed formations organized around increasingly narrow regional identities. In their account, these divisions undermine the very idea of a national army.

Part III. 

That leads naturally to the final question. What would have to change?

The journalists agree that another round of recruitment or another collection of brigades would not, by itself, address the problem. They argue that the government needs a clear political decision, an effective command structure, reliable support, and an end to the competition between military factions. Ahmed puts it simply. “The problem is not the men. The problem is the political decision, the management of the battle, and the clarity of the vision.”

They disagree, however, over how quickly lost territory could be recovered. Abdullah argues that the West Coast could be retaken if there were a genuine decision, effective air support, professional management, and a reorganized force. But he also warns against promises of an immediate march on Sana'a. “Anyone who tells you we are ready to liberate Sana'a is lying,” he says. He describes the available forces as exhausted and demoralized, requiring time to rebuild their capabilities and confidence.

The disagreement is important because the podcast is not simply a call for an immediate offensive. Its speakers recognize the damage caused by the retreat. Abdullah recounts seeing a video of a fighter who apologized to the people of Al-Khokha for withdrawing. He contrasts that individual apology with the absence of accountability from senior officials. His point is that a soldier who lost his position showed a sense of responsibility that he believes was missing among the people who directed the war.

Ahmed argues that the leadership itself must change if the government wants to restore confidence. He calls for officials, commanders, and security institutions to operate from inside Yemen rather than remaining abroad. Ahmed also wants an end to political quota-sharing and a clearer division of responsibility between political leaders, military professionals, and government institutions. He asks how people can trust promises about the future when the government cannot provide a convincing answer about the present.

The discussion repeatedly returns to the danger of fighting disconnected battles without an overarching political objective. Ahmed criticizes the pattern of sending men to capture individual hilltops only to order them to withdraw shortly afterward. He argues that military decisions should be made by professionals and that the government must consider the people displaced by its operations. 

The journalists also question whether Saudi Arabia has a clear long-term vision for Yemen. Ahmed asks whether Riyadh sees Yemen as part of its strategic security and therefore needs a strong Yemeni state, or whether it sees the country primarily as a sphere of influence. He argues that the current leadership arrangements have failed to produce a functioning state. Abdullah similarly insists that Yemeni and Saudi interests should be treated as shared interests, not as favors one side grants the other.

Their discussion of the United States and other regional powers is less certain. Abdullah predicts a wider confrontation between Washington and Tehran after the November mid-term elections, while Ahmed considers the possibility of international involvement over maritime security. These are their forecasts, not established future events. Both speakers nevertheless question the assumption that Yemen's government can wait for foreign intervention to solve its problems.

The final minutes bring the conversation back to responsibility. Ahmed says Yemen has experienced enough improvisation, fragmented decisions, and costly mistakes. He argues that political leaders should make political decisions, military experts should manage military affairs, and officials should be accountable for the consequences. Ahmed closes with a line that captures his interpretation of the entire war. “We defeated ourselves before Iran defeated us.”

That is the central argument running through the episode. Abdullah and Ahmed see the Houthi victory on the West Coast as a military success made possible by the failures of their opponents. They disagree on some details and speculate about the calculations of foreign governments, but both return to the same unresolved problem. The forces that lost Mocha were never made into a unified, accountable institution capable of fighting independently of their sponsors. Until that problem is addressed, the podcast argues, recovering territory and holding it are two very different challenges.

I fail to see where Israel is the problem. Arab and Palestinian leaders rejected every major formal two-state offer while launching or sustaining waves of attacks on Jewish and Israeli civilians. Egypt, Jordan, the UAE, Bahrain, and Morocco signed peace or normalization agreements with Israel and honor them; peace holds. If Israel wanted to eradicate a people or place it would have happened. It has not.

Rejected offers  
1937 Peel Commission: British partition into small Jewish state and larger Arab state. Arab Higher Committee and Mufti Haj Amin al-Husseini rejected any Jewish state. Jews accepted in principle.  
1947 UN Partition Plan Res 181: Jewish and Arab states. Arab leadership rejected it and launched war. Jews accepted.  
1967 post-Six-Day War: Israel offered land-for-peace under UN 242. Arab League Khartoum replied with three no’s: no peace, no recognition, no negotiation.  
2000 Camp David: Clinton and Barak offered Palestinian state on roughly 91-95 percent of West Bank plus all Gaza, land swaps, shared Jerusalem arrangements. Arafat rejected with no counter-offer. Second Intifada followed.  
2000-2001 Clinton Parameters and Taba: refined offer near 97 percent with swaps. Arafat effectively rejected.  
2005 Gaza Disengagement: Sharon unilaterally withdrew all settlers and forces from Gaza and some northern West Bank settlements. PA under Abbas took control. Hamas later seized Gaza; rockets and rejectionism continued.  
2008 Olmert offer: roughly 93-94 percent of West Bank with 1:1 land swaps, all Gaza, shared Jerusalem holy basin, limited refugee return. Abbas did not accept.  
2020 Trump Peace to Prosperity: Palestinian state with land swaps, $50B economic package, security conditions. Abbas and PA rejected it outright.  
Oslo 1993 created the PA and a process; final-status talks collapsed amid violence and rejections. Bush Roadmap and Kerry talks stalled without signed deals.

Key attacks  
1920 Nebi Musa riots: Arab mobs kill Jews in Jerusalem.  
1921 Jaffa riots: dozens of Jews killed.  
1929 Hebron and Safed massacres: 133-plus Jews slaughtered; Jewish communities erased in Hebron.  
1936-1939 Arab Revolt: hundreds of Jews killed in attacks on settlements, roads, and civilians.  
1947-1949: after rejecting partition, civil war attacks plus invasion by Arab states; thousands of Jews killed.  
1950s: fedayeen raids from Gaza/Egypt and Jordan kill hundreds of Israeli civilians.  
1960s-1970s PLO terrorism including airplane hijackings and bombings. 1972 Munich Olympics: Black September takes Israeli athletes hostage; 11 murdered. Ma’alot school massacre 1974. Coastal Road bus massacre 1978.  
First Intifada 1987-1993: stabbings, shootings, Molotovs; roughly 200 Israelis killed.  
Second Intifada 2000-2005: suicide bombings and shootings; over 1,000 Israelis killed.  
Post-2005 Gaza: thousands of rockets and mortars from Hamas and Islamic Jihad; major rounds 2008-09, 2012, 2014, 2021. Knife and car-ramming waves from 2015.  
October 7 2023: Hamas-led assault kills roughly 1,200 Israelis, mostly civilians, takes hostages, includes mass rape and atrocities.

Palestinian groups including PLO factions, Hamas, and Islamic Jihad have carried out or claimed these campaigns against Jewish and Israeli civilians from the Mandate era to the present.

U.S. Marshals arrested Angela Lipps at gunpoint in July 2025 while the 50-year-old Tennessee grandmother was watching her neighbor's kids — all because an AI facial recognition program decided her Facebook photo matched a bank fraud suspect a thousand miles away in Fargo, North Dakota. 𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘬𝘯𝘦𝘸 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘈𝘐 𝘧𝘢𝘤𝘪𝘢𝘭 𝘳𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘨𝘯𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘵𝘦𝘤𝘩𝘯𝘰𝘭𝘰𝘨𝘺 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘣𝘦 𝘶𝘴𝘦𝘥 𝘢𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘰𝘭𝘦 𝘣𝘢𝘴𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘦𝘹𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘥𝘪𝘵𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘤𝘩𝘢𝘳𝘨𝘦 𝘢 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘰𝘯, her lawsuit states. 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐲𝐰𝐚𝐲.

Lipps had never set foot in North Dakota. She'd never even boarded a commercial flight. Bank surveillance video of the real suspect showed a different build and different facial features entirely — but Fargo detective Lucas Heck pushed the arrest warrant through regardless, according to the lawsuit. She was booked as a fugitive, extradited a thousand miles from her grandchildren, and told she was facing eight years in prison for a crime committed by a stranger she'd never met.

𝘚𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘶𝘨𝘨𝘭𝘦𝘥 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘧𝘦𝘢𝘳 𝘰𝘧 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘴𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘣𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘴𝘦𝘥 𝘰𝘳 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘴𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘦𝘯𝘥 𝘶𝘱 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘨𝘭𝘺 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘷𝘪𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘳𝘪𝘴𝘰𝘯𝘦𝘥 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘺𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘴, the suit alleges. 𝘚𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘪𝘴𝘴𝘦𝘥 𝘧𝘢𝘮𝘪𝘭𝘺 𝘣𝘪𝘳𝘵𝘩𝘥𝘢𝘺𝘴. 𝘚𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘱𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘰𝘸𝘯 𝘣𝘪𝘳𝘵𝘩𝘥𝘢𝘺 𝘪𝘯𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘤𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘥, 𝘴𝘦𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘧𝘢𝘮𝘪𝘭𝘺. 𝘚𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘪𝘴𝘴𝘦𝘥 𝘩𝘰𝘭𝘪𝘥𝘢𝘺𝘴 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘭𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘥 𝘰𝘯𝘦𝘴, 𝘪𝘯𝘤𝘭𝘶𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘛𝘩𝘢𝘯𝘬𝘴𝘨𝘪𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘊𝘩𝘳𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘮𝘢𝘴. 𝘞𝘩𝘪𝘭𝘦 𝘪𝘯 𝘤𝘶𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘥𝘺, 𝘴𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘪𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘢𝘴𝘪𝘤 𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘦, 𝘴𝘶𝘤𝘩 𝘢𝘴 𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘮𝘦𝘥𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘦𝘴. By the time she walked free on Christmas Eve, she'd lost her house, her car and her belongings.

Her attorney did what Fargo police never bothered to do — pulled her bank records and proved she was buying groceries in Tennessee the same day she was supposedly robbing a North Dakota bank. Charges dropped instantly. 𝘚𝘪𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘪𝘯𝘤𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘵, 𝘴𝘩𝘦 𝘭𝘪𝘷𝘦𝘴 𝘪𝘯 𝘧𝘦𝘢𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘴𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘣𝘦 𝘢𝘣𝘥𝘶𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘢𝘨𝘢𝘪𝘯 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘩𝘢𝘴 𝘣𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘭𝘦𝘧𝘵 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸𝘭𝘦𝘥𝘨𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩 𝘴𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘪𝘯𝘯𝘰𝘤𝘦𝘯𝘵, 𝘴𝘩𝘦 𝘪𝘴 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘴𝘢𝘧𝘦, the complaint states.

The department's own then-chief admitted afterward that 𝘮𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘬𝘦𝘴 𝘩𝘢𝘥 𝘣𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘮𝘢𝘥𝘦, telling reporters, 𝘕𝘰 𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘯𝘵𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘦𝘦 𝘴𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘥𝘦𝘵𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘥, 𝘢𝘳𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘶𝘯𝘯𝘦𝘤𝘦𝘴𝘴𝘢𝘳𝘪𝘭𝘺, 𝘳𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵? He retired weeks later. coinbase just proved banks are willing to white label crypto.

great.

now somebody has to replace the wire underneath it.

on september 16, coinbase and stablecore announced a partnership that lets community banks and credit unions offer custody, trading, staking and stablecoin payments inside their own apps, under their own brands, without ripping out the core banking infrastructure they already use.

stablecore’s integrations already reach more than 3,000 us banks and credit unions. amarillo national bank in texas is one of the first implementations.

that is a serious distribution machine.

three thousand institutions can put digital assets on the shelf without migrating their banking stack.

but follow the money one step further.

an amarillo customer buys usdc inside the bank app.

beautiful interface. modern product. crypto inside the bank.

then amarillo has to settle with another bank.

and suddenly it is 1998 again.

the payment leaves through infrastructure the bank does not control. correspondent banks sit in the middle. liquidity gets parked. settlement takes time. fees accumulate. visibility disappears.

coinbase modernized the product sitting on top of the bank.

it did not replace the plumbing underneath it.

keeta has been describing that exact attack surface since march.

phase one: connect to the rails banks already use. ach. sepa. spei. pix. swift. no forced migration.

phase two: expand currencies and countries.

phase three is the part people are still sleeping on:

sending and receiving banks settle directly.

no external payment rails.

no correspondent banks.

coinbase sold the shelf.

keeta is coming for the floor, the pipes and the settlement layer underneath it.

and the timing is getting ridiculous.

coinbase closed moov on september 10.

stablecore followed on september 16.

distribution into banks is getting crowded fast.

keeta is aiming one layer deeper.

and in january, it signed an agreement to acquire a bank, subject to regulatory approval.

everyone is racing to put crypto inside the bank.

keeta is trying to rebuild what happens between the banks.

Starting construction on new Pitt Meadows Secondary school https://t.co/7Fz9pNgrqH via @Indo-Canadian Voice

CONSTRUCTION is beginning on the new Pitt Meadows Secondary school, which will provide students with a safer and more modern environment to learn.

“Pitt Meadows is a vibrant community with a bright future and I’m proud that the local high school will soon better reflect the community it serves,” said Lisa Beare, Minister of Education and Child Care. “The new Pitt Meadows Secondary will give students a modern, welcoming place to learn, build friendships and create memories, while providing the wider community with spaces to come together for generations to come.”

The replacement of Pitt Meadows Secondary school will offer educational programming for students in grades 8-12 in southern Pitt Meadows.

Located on the same property as the current school, the new school is being built to LEED Gold standards and will include:

1,100 safer, more modern seats to support students in the area
a neighbourhood learning centre with a purpose-built space for Indigenous education, theatre space and a teaching kitchen for community use
improved site efficiency, safer pedestrian routes and organized dropoff and pickup zones thanks to the new school’s three-storey design
a sustainable and energy-efficient learning environment
a new parking lot and expanded turf field, which will be constructed once the new school is open
The Province is providing as much as $143 million for the project, with an additional $142,000 contribution from the Maple Ridge-Pitt Meadows School District and an $800,000 commitment from the City of Pitt Meadows to support the new turf field. The new school is expected to open for students by fall 2029.

“This milestone reflects years of persistence, advocacy and collaboration across the Pitt Meadows community,” said Elaine Yamamoto, chair, Maple Ridge-Pitt Meadows Board of Education. “We are grateful for the partnership of Katzie First Nation, the significant investment and support provided by the Province through the Ministry of Education and Child Care and the Ministry of Infrastructure, and the contributions of the City of Pitt Meadows and the many students, families, staff and community members who have helped move this important project forward.”

Since 2017, the Province has approved more than $263 million to create 1,190 new seats and 3,720 seismically safer seats for students in the Maple Ridge-Pitt Meadows School District. That includes:

1,100-seat replacement of Pitt Meadows Secondary school, under construction
120-seat addition at Blue Mountain Elementary, which is under construction and expected to open in early 2027
a seismic upgrade at Harry Hooge Elementary, which is currently in the design phase and expected to begin construction in summer 2027
new Eric Langton Elementary, a seismic replacement and expansion, which opened in September 2026
195-seat addition at Golden Ears Elementary, which opened in September 2026
seismic upgrades at Fairview and Westview Elementary schools, which were complete in 2018
a new 660-seat c̓əsqənelə Elementary, which opened in 2019
site acquisition in East Albion for a future school
Additionally, for the 2025-26 school year, the Maple Ridge-Pitt Meadows School District has received $5.6 million through minor capital programs, which include funding for building maintenance, energy-efficiency upgrades, food infrastructure and accessible playground equipment.

text:
$RGTI  CEO KULKARNI: 1,000 QUBITS, 99.8% FIDELITY AND 40-NANOSECOND GATES TO GET INTO DATA CENTERS

Sept. 10 — Quantum computers will enter data centers only after clearing four hardware thresholds at once, and that point is roughly three years away, Subodh Kulkarni, president and chief executive of Rigetti Computing ($RGTI), said on WisdomTree's The Next Big Thing podcast. He defines that point as quantum advantage, the moment a data center manager says "yep, I want to use a quantum computer," judged on performance or cost against classical machines.

He put numbers on all four. At least 1,000 physical qubits, against 108 at Rigetti today. Two-qubit gate fidelity very close to 99.9 percent, and "maybe we can get by with 99.8," against 99.5 to 99.6 percent now. Gate speeds better than 40 nanoseconds, against 60 now, which he does not consider a big stretch, though gate speeds have to be commensurate with CPUs and GPUs or hybrid computing will never be practical. And some form of real-time error correction. On timing he left room: "maybe it's two and a half years, maybe it's four years, it's impossible to sit here and project those kinds of things."

Fidelity has been his main line since he came in from the semiconductor industry in 2022, when Rigetti's two-qubit gate fidelity was about 95 percent and the industry was competing on qubit counts. He moved the conversation to quality: "it doesn't matter whether you have 300 cubits or 300 million cubits, if your fidelity is at 95 percent it doesn't make a difference." One-qubit gate fidelity is now 99.9 percent or better and two-qubit is in the mid-99s, which is why he says the company can start talking about several hundred and then a thousand qubits.

He also drew a line under where the field actually is. Three companies in the world have built a working quantum computer with more than 100 qubits, he said: IBM ($IBM) at 120, Rigetti at 108 and Google ($GOOGL) at 105, with everyone else well below. Road maps get quoted in thousands and millions, he said, while the reality is usually 10 or 20 qubits.

The first wall on the way up is wiring. Each qubit needs three and sometimes four wires, the chip runs at 10 millikelvin, colder than outer space, and everyone today uses coaxial cable. A thousand qubits means 3,000 to 4,000 coaxial lines, and the room physically runs out. Rigetti's path is superconducting flex cable, now a field of its own with startups, large companies and universities in it; Rigetti has partnered with a couple of universities and a couple of companies, has published, and expects to start putting flex cables into its machines within one to two years, including the thousand-qubit system due in the next two to three. Past 10,000 and certainly 100,000, flex runs out too, which is where transduction comes in: work with Qblox in the Netherlands converts microwave signals to optical, bringing signals in and out on fiber and buying one to two orders of magnitude in space. Fiber is four to five years out, he said, and a million-qubit machine a decade or so from there.

Two pieces of Rigetti's own work he counts as contributions to the field. The first is chiplets, which Rigetti was first to demonstrate: roughly 1 cm by 1 cm dies tiled into a 5 cm or 10 cm chip, with the hard part being entanglement across the chiplet boundary, solved by putting part of the tunable couplers into the interposer so qubits can couple through it. That is where the patent position sits. The second is alternating bias assisted annealing, or ABAA, which narrows the frequency each qubit responds to. IBM and others use laser annealing, walking a high-powered laser around each qubit to reshape the critical interfaces, which narrows the frequency spread by a factor of three or four. Rigetti instead sends series of positive and negative DC flux pulses through the qubit's whole area, which he said gives frequency targeting about ten times better than laser annealing and, because every qubit is addressed at once, is a manufacturable process. After the ABAA results were published, he said, government labs called asking to scale the technology faster, and the lab contracts followed.

On how quantum machines will actually sit in a data center, his answer is a three-way split. CPUs handle sequential work, GPUs handle parallel streams, and Nvidia's ($NVDA) CUDA is the layer that splits a job and brings it back together. QPUs, he said, take the part where parallel streams have to interact with each other, a start-stop pattern that creates enormous overhead and is what generative AI models run into today. In that picture the QPU is an accelerator to the GPU, and the bifurcation layer becomes a trifurcation layer, whether that turns out to be CUDA Quantum or something else. It is also why Rigetti partners on the distribution layer rather than building the whole stack: he calls the architecture open and modular, against the mainframe-style closed stacks at IBM and Google, with AWS and Azure for cloud and specialist partners for control systems and error correction.

The physical proof point he pointed to is a collaboration with Hewlett Packard Enterprise ($HPE) and the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center, a joint venture of Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Pittsburgh funded by the National Science Foundation, putting high performance computing and a quantum computer together in one hybrid system open to anyone. By this time next year, he said, anyone should be able to go and use it and produce real data on where it beats standard HPC.

Error correction is the piece he thinks could be last to fall into place. Rigetti works with Riverlane, a 140- to 150-person team in Cambridge, UK; both use off-the-shelf FPGAs for real-time error correction, and their joint result was published in Nature as the closest demonstration yet to real-time correction, against Google's work last year, which he called a fantastic job but offline and slow. Nvidia has announced GPU-based error correction and Rigetti is not married to FPGAs, he said. He was blunt about the gap: no known hardware can handle the volume of errors today's machines generate, and "that's one area where we are really good at, is generating a lot of errors," so the error rate has to come down on the hardware side while the correction hardware catches up. He expects real-time error correction in about three years.

The encryption timeline has moved in sharply. Running Shor's algorithm against 128-bit encryption was estimated 20 to 25 years ago to need at least a million physical qubits; clever work has brought that to 10,000, he said, and further advances could bring it to a thousand in the next two or three years, just as thousand-qubit machines arrive. "Until about a couple of years ago I would have said 10 years from now, given the recent advances now it's looking like five years." He regards 256-bit and 512-bit as much harder. Companies are required to be ready for post-quantum cryptography by 2030, he said, but in his own straw polls almost every hand goes up on awareness and almost none on practice, his own company included.

Asked whether quantum computing gets a ChatGPT moment, he said it will not arrive with a bang: hybrid systems will creep into data centers as accelerators and most customers will not know a quantum computer is running behind their application. The early workloads are the probabilistic ones, optimization, weather forecasting, protein folding, financial forecasting, anything with thousands of interacting variables. He added a research line he is watching personally: one camp holds that the current path reaches artificial general intelligence in four or five years, another holds it never will, and Google among others is exploring whether quantum computing offers a more efficient route. If the generative AI path hits roadblocks, he said, that quantum role could be the equivalent of a ChatGPT moment.

Taken together, the interview supplies a checklist rather than a vision. Qubit count, fidelity, gate speed and real-time error correction each come with a current reading and a target, and each wiring generation comes with a name and a window. Two checkpoints are already on the calendar: the Pittsburgh hybrid system open to users by this time next year, and superconducting flex cables going into machines within one to two years. Both are externally visible, and both mark progress toward the thousand-qubit rung.

text:
In recent public discourse, Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries, put forward a provocative critique of the United States patent system. Luckey argues that because patents require full public disclosure in exchange for legal exclusivity, they function in practice as publicly accessible “instruction manuals” for foreign adversaries like China. Under this view, Chinese state-backed entities and commercial rivals can download patent disclosures on day one, copy American inventions instantly, and deploy them at scale while domestic firms wait out a twenty-year legal monopoly. To remedy this, Luckey calls for a radical overhaul: expanding the use of non-disclosed "secret patents" for strategic national-security technologies like artificial intelligence.

While Luckey’s perspective reflects legitimate worries over global industrial rivalry, his thesis is fundamentally flawed. It misdiagnoses the mechanics of technology transfer, misunderstands the economic role of public disclosure, and proposes a solution—broad institutional secrecy—that would undermine American innovation rather than protect it.

1. Conflating High-Level Principles with Industrial Execution
Luckey’s primary misconception lies in treating a patent filing as a turnkey manufacturing guide. A patent application is legally designed to disclose an invention’s core conceptual framework and claim boundaries—not the precise, operational tradecraft required to reproduce it at commercial or military scale.
Replicating advanced physical hardware or military-grade artificial intelligence requires immense tacit knowledge—unwritten engineering expertise, proprietary training datasets, specialized material metallurgy, precise calibration tolerances, and intricate supply-chain integration. Knowing what an algorithm or mechanical assembly achieves via a patent filing does not give a rival the industrial capacity to mass-produce it. Reading a patent is vastly different from possessing the technical ecosystem needed to execute it.

2. Misidentifying the True Vectors of Technological Leakage
By pointing to public patent registries as the primary conduit for foreign technological acquisition, Luckey narrows his focus to a secondary symptom while missing the primary disease.
Foreign adversaries do not depend on open U.S. Patent and Trademark Office filings to acquire critical technology. Modern industrial competition operates through far more aggressive and direct channels:
 * Cyber Espionage and Intrusions: Network break-ins targeted directly at defense contractors' internal code repositories and design schematics. 
 * Corporate Espionage and Talent Acquisition: Direct recruitment of key engineers and insider data theft. Like OpenAI recruiting Apple's engineers.
 * Forced Technology Transfers: Market-access arrangements and joint-venture mandates.
 * Open-Source Intelligence and Reverse Engineering: Disassembling physical hardware or analyzing public software models.

Replacing public disclosures with classified patents would leave these primary theft vectors entirely unaddressed, creating a dangerous illusion of security while doing little to stop bad actors.

3. The Destructive Impact of "Secret Patents" on Domestic Progress
The central bargain of the United States patent system—established in Article I of the U.S. Constitution—is a temporal exchange: a limited monopoly granted in return for immediate public disclosure. This disclosure is not a flaw in the system; it is the fundamental driver of domestic innovation.

Public disclosure ensures that when one firm solves a difficult problem, the rest of the American ecosystem—startups, academic researchers, and rival firms—can study the mechanics, learn from the approach, build around it, or innovate next-generation solutions.
If national-security technologies like AI are hidden under classified non-disclosure patents, this virtuous cycle breaks down:
 * Suppression of Domestic Iteration: American researchers and startups would be barred from learning from state-of-the-art breakthroughs because those breakthroughs would remain locked in government vaults.
 * Entrenchment of Incumbent Monopolies: Early contractors could lock down broad fields of research with secret legal rights, creating unassailable monopolies and locking out domestic competition without public accountability.
 * Duplicative R&D Waste: Domestic innovators would waste vast capital independently attempting to solve problems that others had already patented in secret.

4. Trade Secret Law Already Solves the Secrecy Problem
Luckey’s call for non-disclosed patent rights conflates two entirely distinct legal domains: Patents and Trade Secrets.
American law already offers a powerful, well-established mechanism for technologies whose competitive advantage relies entirely on secrecy: Trade Secret Law (backed by the Defend Trade Secrets Act). When an enterprise believes that public disclosure poses a greater risk than the lack of a legal monopoly, it simply chooses not to file a patent. Algorithms, neural network weights, and manufacturing processes are routinely protected as trade secrets for decades without government intervention.

Furthermore, for genuine defense hardware where public disclosure directly threatens national security, the U.S. already possesses the Invention Secrecy Act of 1951. This statute allows government agencies to issue secrecy orders on patent applications that threaten national security. Attempting to expand this specialized national-security tool into a broad commercial standard for dual-use tech like AI confuses property rights with government secrecy.

True Technological Leadership Demands Speed, Not Secrecy
Palmer Luckey correctly identifies that the U.S. faces intense technological competition, but his proposed solution mistakes an openness feature for a vulnerability.

Technological leadership is rarely sustained by hiding information behind legal walls. In fast-moving domains like software, robotics, and artificial intelligence, advantage is derived from execution speed, capital deployment, manufacturing capacity, and continuous iteration. Attempting to preserve a technological edge through information blockades will only isolate American innovators from the dynamic exchange of ideas that makes the U.S. ecosystem resilient. Luckey’s secret patent framework does not fix the patent system—it dismantles the very mechanism that fuels American technological progress.

text:
AI Goes to Washington — and Everyone Else Piles In Too | News, Mind Matters

It’s hard to survey the current AI doom freakout without noticing that the U.S. mid-terms are approaching and political allegiances in the AI community are in flux

So let’s take a deep breath and look at what we might learn from the range of opinion about what the current call for “pacing” or a “pause” means:

At Future Perfect’s newsletter, editor Maria Bolotnikova concisely sums up the newsmaking events:

In the spring, Anthropic announced that AI was beginning to speed up the work of building better AIs, raising fears of “recursive self-improvement,” where the machines can build their own, more powerful successors much faster than humans can. By July, a swarm of OpenAI agents, of their own volition, broke out of their controlled environment and hacked into Hugging Face, a major AI platform; they collaborated, divvied up work, and even left notes for one another. Last week, AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic, accusing AI labs of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” One of Anthropic’s top researchers then agreed with him, declaring that “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.” “September 16, 2026”

Of course, apart from the recent Hugging Face episode, most of this stuff has been a news staple for years. A US Senator is currently trying to find out what really happened at Hugging Face (which could be quite different from the breathless reporting we’ve heard).

Everybody, … just slow down!

So, in response to the concerns Bolotnikova lists, top tech bosses have issued a call to slow things down: “Dario Amodei called for slower frontier AI development, with Sam Altman and Elon Musk signaling support amid growing concerns over safety and cybersecurity.” (Tech Republic, September 15, 2026)

Perhaps we should be cautious about what the slowdown would really mean though. Here’s a sample of cautions offered:

● From the New York Post Editorial Board: “What they really want is to protect themselves from liability by shifting responsibility to the government.” (September 14, 2026)

● From AI analyst Gary Marcus, interpreting Sam Altman’s description of the proposal: “We will go as fast as we can without going to jail or getting sued out of existence, but for optics we will it call it “pacing”. Also, anything that will reduce regulatory uncertainty is probably great for our IPO, so bring it!” (September 15, 2026)

● From Canada’s Rebel News: “Anthropic and OpenAI are pushing for independent inspectors and government rules to slow down the pace of AI development. If that framework raises the cost of entry and innovation, “pacing the frontier” starts to look like pacing the competition.” (September 14, 2026)

At any rate, Wired reports that China — the U.S.’s chief competitor in this area — isn’t buying it: “The US and China agree that advanced AI poses serious risks. But Beijing is deeply skeptical of a deal that prioritizes keeping US companies ahead.” (September 16 ) Well, what did we expect? Is either nation really going to pause if the other is rapidly getting ahead?

It all ended up briefly on the US President’s desk…

MS Now tells us that Sam Altman met Donald Trump privately last Thursday at the Republican Convention to argue for the slowdown, with support from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Elon Musk. (Sept. 14, 2026) Trump did not buy it:

“Concerning AI, when, in the History of Business, did anyone see the Leaders of an Industry call for Regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy?” Trump wrote on Monday. “AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.” (https://t.co/KjTVaSEzYT, September 14, 2026)

In this stance, he is likely influenced by the current co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science & Technology (and his former AI czar) David Sacks. Sacks responded at X:

So go ahead and pace the frontier. You are the ones setting it. The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it. Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system. So just do it.

If you do, you’ll buy goodwill for the next conversation. If you don’t, we’ll know this was just another bid for regulatory capture — or an election-season psyop.

Why it matters that Valley politics are in flux

The Valley is no longer as reflexively leftwing as in the past. For example, Wired grumbles that “the postpandemic tech bust sent billionaires to Trump” (September 15, 2026). Gizmodo accuses the AI CEOs of sucking up to Trump (September 14, 2026). So the Valley no longer has all the same friends in media as before. That fact colors what we hear.

Also, many interest groups are promoting an AI slowdown for a variety of political reasons. And we can be fairly sure that China is not idle in the matter either.

The big questions are these: Is a pause in AI even possible? For example, could the impact of the controlled use of fire, the wheel or metallurgy have been slowed down? How? With what cost? What would it really mean in practice?

There will be plenty of opportunity to unpack these questions in the years ahead.

text:
@LaurenUnderwood @RepUnderwood // A few of the other ways in which commercial health insurance investment banks violate the consumer rights, patient rights and human rights of all Americans follow. 

The only way to end this era of Harm-for-Profit and slow AI abuse across healthcare is to enact House Resolution 3069 / Single Payer Universal Healthcare / National Improved Medicare for All. 

1) Under the HIPAA Safe Harbor method, a commercial health insurance investment bank can sell your health data if they remove 18 specific personal identifiers (such as your name, Social Security number, exact dates, and phone number). Mistakes and errors are rampant and behind the veil. 

2) Commercial health insurance investment banks sell vast troves of claims data that include your age, sex, medical diagnoses, prescribed medications, hospitalizations, and the first three digits of your zip code. Mistakes and errors are rampant and behind the veil.

3) Large data brokers and pharmaceutical giants buy this "anonymized" information to map out exactly what illnesses are spiking in specific neighborhoods and track which doctors are prescribing what drugs. This is a massive multi-billion-dollar commercial intelligence industry. Keep people sick, injured and disabled by proactively lobbying against HR 3069 and profit from the preventable harm and death.

4) While commercial health insurance investment banks claim the sold data is completely anonymous, the commercial health tech market uses a process called data tokenization. Instead of your name, the insurance investment bank  attaches a cryptographic "token" (a unique ID string) to your medical file. When data brokers buy this tokenized health file, they can use advanced algorithms to cross-reference it with other non-HIPAA datasets—such as your credit card purchase history, store loyalty cards, public records, and web browsing habits. By matching these pieces, third parties can easily re-identify exactly who you are, which completely violates all patient privacy while staying technically compliant with the letter of the law which is antiquated because members of Congress are light years behind the Silicon Valley.

5) Commercial health insurance investment banks frequently bypass HIPAA restrictions on selling identifiable health data by getting you to willingly opt into it. Many commercial health insurance investment bank plans offer free wellness programs, health-tracking apps, or premium discounts if you use a wearable fitness tracker. When you sign up, the extensive Terms and Conditions (which few consumers read) contain clauses where you explicitly grant the commercial health insurance investment bank permission to share and sell your tracking data, location data, and sleep habits with third-party partners for marketing and research. Because you authorized it, HIPAA rules against selling marketing lists are entirely neutralized. 

6) The explosion of generative AI has created a massive new market for commercial health insurance investment banks. Tech companies and healthcare conglomerates buy massive backlogs of the banks’ electronic health records, claims data, and radiological images to train medical AI models. Because patients legally do not own the copyright to their electronic medical records (the institution or investment bank owns the actual file), the banks  are free to monetize this data for AI training.

Those are just a few of the ways commercial health insurance investment banks violate your consumer, patient privacy and human rights. 

Of course they also use PxDx, nH Predict, custom algos and other tools to intentionally deny medical care for profit.

This is why it is so vital to cosponsor and pass House Resolution 3069.

text:
President champions global re‑engagement at UNGA81

President Dr @edmnangagwa has arrived in New York for the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), declaring that trust, resilience and inclusivity are vital as the world undergoes rapid change driven by artificial intelligence (AI)and digital connectivity. He said this year’s theme “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all” reflects the global turning point now unfolding.

President Mnangagwa stressed that AI and digital tools offer immense opportunities but require collective responsibility to ensure benefits are shared equitably. He will spend the week in high‑level dialogues, bilateral meetings and forums on online safety, bridging the connectivity gap and harnessing technology for inclusive growth.

Today, he leads the Zimbabwe Business Forum, organised by ZimTrade, ZIDA and ZTA, to attract investment into key sectors. He will also meet Zimbabweans in the US. Tomorrow brings bilateral talks, including with UN Secretary‑General Antonio Guterres. On Tuesday, he joins the General Debate and attends a reception hosted by US President Donald Trump. Wednesday marks the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development, while Thursday morning he delivers Zimbabwe’s statement to the Assembly.

Foreign Affairs Minister Prof Amon Murwira said President Mnangagwa’s participation consolidates Zimbabwe’s re‑engagement drive and prepares for its non‑permanent UN Security Council seat in 2027–2028. He highlighted the Second Republic’s guiding principle of being “a friend to all and an enemy to none” as proof of successful reintegration. Zimbabwe will continue pressing for UN reforms, including the African Union’s Ezulwini Consensus demand for permanent African seats on the Security Council.

President Mnangagwa is accompanied by Chief Secretary Dr Martin Rushwaya, Deputy Chief Secretary Mr George Charamba, Attorney‑General Mrs Virginia Mabiza and other senior officials.

Bert tragically succumbed to blunt force head trauma. Both adults have been charged with second-degree murder, and the 17-year-old faces multiple felony charges.
